Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- The question is starting to feel a little old: Whom will Barack Obama pick as his vice president? Sen. Barack Obama has a big event scheduled Saturday. Will his No. 2 man (or woman) be by his side? With the clock ticking (the Democratic VP candidate delivers a big speech next Wednesday) the announcement is at most days and at least a few hours away. Everyday seems to be "the day," the day the guessing game will finally end. In a poke at all of the VP buzz, the Obama campaign sent an e-mail to reporters Wednesday with the subject line "Vice presidential ..." The first line of the e-mail: "Just kidding." The e-mail contained details about Obama's schedule with no mention of any of the potential vice presidential candidates. But if the top contenders have any inside information, they're doing a good job of keeping quiet. Sen. Joe Biden told reporters camped outside his Delaware home Tuesday that it's not him. "You got better things to do, guys; I'm not the guy," he said. Asked where he would be Saturday -- when Obama is reportedly scheduled to hold a campaign event in Springfield, Illinois, that may feature his new running mate -- Biden replied, "here," pointing to his driveway. He softened up a little later that night, telling reporters, "I promise you, I don't know anything." Along with Biden, Sen. Evan Bayh of Indiana and Virginia Gov. Tim Kaine are considered to be among the top tier of VP contenders.  Watch the latest on Obama's VP selection » . Bayh has managed to stay out of the spotlight this week. Does that mean he's dodging the question? He hit the Sunday talk show circuit this weekend and tried out the attack dog role, criticizing Republican John McCain for his stance on Georgia, Iraq and national security. When asked about the veepstakes, the former governor said he had "nothing to report today." Kaine, on the other hand, seems to have no qualms about taking the main stage this week. A relative newcomer to national politics, Kaine is scheduled to appear alongside Obama on Thursday as the presumptive Democratic nominee campaigns in central Virginia. Could he be introduced as Obama's No. 2 man? The pair will host an invitation-only town hall meeting Thursday in Chesterfield County, a suburb of Richmond. Kaine's sturdy performance in the traditionally conservative Richmond suburbs helped vault him to the governorship in 2005. Obama has stops scheduled in Virginia on Wednesday and Thursday before returning home to Illinois for the Springfield event, which takes place where he first kicked off his presidential run. The event marks the beginning of a tour of battleground states leading into next week's convention in Denver, Colorado. The Obama campaign has kept the details on both the timing and selection of the running mate under wraps. They would neither confirm or deny whether Obama would appear with his VP candidate this weekend. iReport.com: Whom do you think Obama should pick? Although the focus in recent days has been on Bayh, Biden and Kaine, there are quite a few other serious contenders, and a curveball pick could always be in the works. Other big names thought to be in the running include retired Gen. Wesley Clark, New York Sen. Hillary Clinton, Connecticut Sen. Chris Dodd, Texas Rep. Chet Edwards, Nebraska Sen. Chuck Hagel, Virginia Gov. Tim Kaine, former Georgia Sen. Sam Nunn, Rhode Island Sen. Jack Reed, New Mexico Gov. Bill Richardson and Kansas Gov. Kathleen Sebelius. Obama's campaign says that when he makes up his mind, he'll send a text message and e-mail to his supporters to let them know who his sidekick will be.

It contained details about Obama’s schedule but made no mention of any potential vice presidential candidates.

If the leading contenders have any inside information, however, they are doing a good job of keeping it quiet.

“You got better things to do, guys; I’m not the guy,” he said.

Asked where he would be Saturday—when Obama is reportedly scheduled to hold a campaign event in Springfield, Illinois, that could feature his new running mate—Biden replied, “here,” pointing to his driveway.

He softened his remarks somewhat later that night, telling reporters, “I promise you, I don’t know anything.”

Along with Biden, Sen. Evan Bayh of Indiana and Virginia Gov. Tim Kaine are considered to be among the top tier of vice presidential contenders.

Watch the latest on Obama’s VP selection »

Bayh has managed to remain out of the spotlight this week. Does that mean he is avoiding the question?

He appeared on the Sunday talk-show circuit this weekend and tried out the attack-dog role, criticizing Republican John McCain for his positions on Georgia, Iraq and national security.

When asked about the vice presidential contest, the former governor said he had “nothing to report today.”

Kaine, by contrast, appears to have no reservations about taking center stage this week.

A relative newcomer to national politics, Kaine is scheduled to appear alongside Obama on Thursday as the presumptive Democratic nominee campaigns in central Virginia.

Could he be introduced as Obama’s No. 2?

The pair will host an invitation-only town hall meeting Thursday in Chesterfield County, a Richmond suburb. Kaine’s strong performance in the traditionally conservative Richmond suburbs helped propel him to the governorship in 2005.

Obama has stops scheduled in Virginia on Wednesday and Thursday before returning home to Illinois for the Springfield event, which will take place where he first launched his presidential campaign.

The event marks the beginning of a tour through battleground states leading into next week’s convention in Denver, Colorado.

The Obama campaign has kept details about both the timing of the announcement and the selection of a running mate under wraps. Campaign officials would neither confirm nor deny whether Obama would appear with his vice presidential candidate this weekend.

Obama’s campaign joked about the intense interest Wednesday by sending reporters an e-mail with the subject line “Vice presidential ...” Its opening words were, “Just kidding.” The message provided information about Obama’s schedule but said nothing about any possible running mate.

Biden, Indiana Sen. Evan Bayh and Virginia Gov. Tim Kaine are widely viewed as leading contenders. Watch the latest developments in Obama’s vice-presidential search.

Bayh has largely avoided public attention this week, raising the possibility that he may be trying to escape questions about the selection. Over the weekend, however, he appeared on several Sunday television programs and took on the traditional running-mate role of political attacker, faulting Republican John McCain’s positions on Georgia, Iraq and national security. Asked about the vice-presidential contest, the former governor said he had “nothing to report today.”

Kaine, by contrast, appears comfortable in the spotlight. Though still relatively new to national politics, he is due to join Obama on Thursday while the presumed Democratic nominee campaigns in central Virginia. That appearance has prompted speculation that Kaine might be presented as Obama’s running mate.

The two are scheduled to lead an invitation-only town hall Thursday in Chesterfield County, outside Richmond. Kaine’s strong showing in Richmond’s traditionally conservative suburbs helped propel him into the governor’s office in 2005.

Obama plans to campaign in Virginia on Wednesday and Thursday, then return to Illinois for the Springfield gathering. That location is where he originally launched his presidential campaign. The event will begin a swing through battleground states ahead of the Democratic convention in Denver, Colorado, the following week.

The Obama organization has disclosed neither when the announcement will come nor whom he will select. Campaign officials would not confirm or deny that Obama might appear beside his vice-presidential nominee over the weekend.

iReport.com asked readers whom they believed Obama should choose.

Although Bayh, Biden and Kaine have attracted most of the recent attention, several other candidates remain under serious consideration, and an unexpected selection is still possible. Other prominent names associated with the search include retired Gen. Wesley Clark; New York Sen. Hillary Clinton; Connecticut Sen. Chris Dodd; Texas Rep. Chet Edwards; Nebraska Sen. Obama’s campaign says that once he reaches a decision, supporters will be notified of his choice by both text message and e-mail.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about speculation surrounding Barack Obama’s imminent 2008 vice-presidential selection, focusing on Joe Biden, Evan Bayh, and Tim Kaine.
counterfactuals.output:
# Obama’s vice-presidential search centers on Biden, Bayh and Kaine

**WASHINGTON (CNN) —** With the Democratic National Convention days away, speculation over Barack Obama’s choice of a running mate is intensifying, with Sens. Joe Biden and Evan Bayh and Virginia Gov. Tim Kaine emerging as leading possibilities.

Obama’s campaign has kept the selection process tightly guarded, offering few clues about when or how the presumptive Democratic nominee will announce his decision. Supporters who signed up for campaign alerts have been told they will be among the first to learn the identity of the vice-presidential nominee.

Each of the three potential choices would bring different strengths to the Democratic ticket.

Biden, a veteran Delaware senator and chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, could add extensive national security and foreign policy credentials. His experience might help answer Republican criticism that Obama, a first-term senator, is not prepared to serve as commander in chief.

But Biden’s long record in Washington could complicate Obama’s campaign message of change. He also sought the Democratic presidential nomination and sharply questioned Obama’s readiness during the primary contest, comments Republicans would be likely to revive.

Bayh, a two-term senator and former Indiana governor, is viewed as a centrist with executive experience and strong political ties in a traditionally Republican state. His selection could signal an effort by Obama to broaden the electoral map and appeal to moderate voters.

Some Democrats, however, question whether Bayh would generate excitement among the party’s base or reinforce Obama’s central argument that the election represents a break from conventional Washington politics.

Kaine, the governor of Virginia and an early Obama supporter, has a close personal and political relationship with the Illinois senator. Fluent in Spanish after working as a missionary in Honduras, Kaine could help the campaign’s outreach to Hispanic voters. His presence on the ticket could also strengthen Democratic prospects in Virginia, which has not backed a Democratic presidential nominee since 1964.

Kaine’s comparatively limited foreign policy experience may be a concern, particularly as the campaign remains focused on the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and tensions with Russia.

Other names have surfaced throughout the search, but attention has increasingly focused on Biden, Bayh and Kaine as Obama approaches a final decision.

The choice will offer one of the clearest indications yet of how Obama intends to frame the general election: Biden would emphasize experience, Bayh could underscore moderation and geographic reach, while Kaine would reinforce the campaign’s themes of generational change and political partnership.

For now, the candidates and their allies are saying little. But with the convention approaching and the campaign preparing a closely watched rollout, Obama’s decision appears imminent.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

**WASHINGTON —** The guessing game over Barack Obama’s running mate intensified as his presidential campaign sent supporters a teasing e-mail promising they would be among the first to learn his choice.

The message urged supporters to sign up for a text-message alert, saying Obama had made—or was close to making—one of the most important decisions of his campaign. But it offered no name or timetable, fueling speculation ahead of the Democratic National Convention.

Asked whether he was the choice, however, Biden denied it, telling reporters, “I’m not the guy.” His foreign-policy experience and long Senate career nevertheless continued to make him a frequently mentioned possibility.

Other names in circulation included Indiana Sen. Evan Bayh, Virginia Gov. Tim Kaine and Kansas Gov. Kathleen Sebelius. Some Democrats also continued to raise New York Sen. counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a breaking-news-style CNN article from August 2008 analyzing when and where Barack Obama might announce his vice-presidential nominee and listing the politicians believed to be under consideration.
counterfactuals.output:
# Obama VP announcement could come within days

**August 20, 2008 — WASHINGTON (CNN)** — Barack Obama could reveal his vice-presidential choice as early as this week, ending months of speculation and setting the Democratic ticket ahead of the party’s national convention in Denver.

The Obama campaign has not disclosed when or where the announcement will be made. But aides have signaled that supporters who registered for text-message alerts will be among the first to learn the identity of the Illinois senator’s running mate.

The timing is increasingly tight. The Democratic National Convention begins Monday, August 25, and Obama is expected to arrive in Denver with his ticket already in place.

One possibility is that Obama will announce his choice at a rally in a politically important battleground state. Another is Springfield, Illinois, where he launched his presidential campaign in February 2007. The city’s Old State Capitol would provide a symbolic backdrop linking the announcement to Obama’s message of political change and national unity.

Obama’s schedule and the movements of potential running mates are being closely watched, although campaign officials have cautioned against reading too much into travel plans.

### The leading possibilities

Several Democrats are believed to remain under consideration:

- **Sen. Joe Biden of Delaware**, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, could add decades of foreign-policy and national-security experience to the ticket. Biden competed against Obama during the Democratic primaries and has become one of the party’s most prominent voices on Iraq and Afghanistan.

- **Sen. Evan Bayh of Indiana**, a former two-term governor, is viewed as a centrist with executive and legislative experience. His selection could help Obama compete in Indiana and appeal to moderate voters across the Midwest.

- **Virginia Gov. Tim Kaine**, an early Obama supporter, could reinforce the campaign’s outsider message and improve Democratic prospects in Virginia, a state that has voted Republican in presidential elections for decades.

- **Kansas Gov. Kathleen Sebelius** has twice won statewide office in heavily Republican territory. Supporters say she would strengthen Obama’s argument that he can bridge partisan divisions, though critics note her limited foreign-policy background.

Other names mentioned in Democratic circles include **Sen. Chris Dodd of Connecticut**, **New Mexico Gov. Bill Richardson** and **retired Gen. Wesley Clark**.

### What about Clinton?

Sen. Hillary Clinton of New York remains the most prominent possible choice after winning nearly 18 million votes during the Democratic nomination fight.

A joint Obama-Clinton ticket could help unify the party and energize Clinton’s supporters. But political observers have questioned whether the two former rivals could form an effective governing partnership after a long and sometimes bitter primary campaign.

Clinton has said the decision belongs to Obama and that she intends to work for his election regardless of whom he chooses.

### What Obama may be looking for

Obama has said he wants a running mate who is prepared to become president and who will challenge his thinking rather than simply agree with him.

That standard could favor a candidate with substantial experience in Washington or foreign affairs, areas Republicans have identified as vulnerabilities for the first-term senator. At the same time, selecting a longtime Washington figure could complicate Obama’s effort to campaign as an agent of change.

With Republican nominee-in-waiting John McCain also considering his vice-presidential choice, Obama’s announcement will open the next phase of the 2008 campaign — and provide voters with their first look at the full Democratic ticket.
